The mosque at the shrine of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (Eyüp Sultan in Turkish), a companion and standard-bearer of Muhammad who is believed to have died here during the first Arab siege of Constantinople in the 670s. It stands in the Eyüp district of Istanbul, by the Golden Horn. Mehmed II built the first mosque complex here in 1458, five years after the conquest, when the tomb was found; by tradition his teacher Akşemseddin had dreamt of the spot.

By the late 18th century the mosque was in ruins, perhaps from earthquakes, and in 1798 Selim III had it pulled down and rebuilt, all but its minarets; the work was finished in 1800. The new mosque keeps the classical plan of a central dome with half domes, in the manner of Sinan, but its gates, mihrab and minbar are carved in the Ottoman Baroque style. An inner courtyard joins the mosque to the domed tomb of Abu Ayyub, whose walls are faced with Iznik tiles, many from about 1580 with the bright red glaze of that period.

Because of its sanctity, a new sultan came here, along the Accession Way, to be girded with the Sword of Osman on a platform under the plane tree in the courtyard, then went on to his ancestor's tomb at the Fatih Mosque. Grand viziers and royal women chose to be buried nearby, and the Eyüp cemetery climbs the hill behind. It is still a place of pilgrimage, and families bring boys here in their finery before circumcision.
